---
title: "How to plot features along the probe"
aliases:
  - ../how-to/plot-features-along-probe.html
---

Electrophysiological features change systematically with depth — that structure is the
whole reason a region decoder can work. This guide plots it three ways: each feature as a
colour-coded strip down one probe beside the brain regions, every feature of a probe as one
z-scored heatmap, and the distribution of every feature across a whole dataset.

Every figure on this page was produced by the code shown, run against the feature tables
committed in this repository at `tests/fixtures/features/2025_W28/` — 13 probes,
384 channels each. The script `examples/plot_features_along_probe.py` draws all of them.

## Prerequisites

- A feature table indexed by `(pid, channel)` — from
  [your own recording](../how-to/compute-features-spikeglx.qmd) or the
  [published aggregates](../how-to/load-channel-features.qmd)
- The matching channel table, carrying `axial_um`, `lateral_um` and `atlas_id`
- `matplotlib`

## Prepare the data

The plotting functions want features and channel geometry in **one** DataFrame, plus a
region-id column in the mapping you want to colour by. Merge on the `(pid, channel)`
index, dropping the columns the two tables share so the merge produces no `_x` / `_y`
suffixes:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions

path = Path("tests/fixtures/features/2025_W28")

df_features = pd.read_parquet(path / "raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt")
df_channels = pd.read_parquet(path / "channels.pqt")

duplicate_cols = set(df_features.columns) & set(df_channels.columns)
df = df_features.merge(
    df_channels.drop(columns=duplicate_cols),
    how="inner",
    left_index=True,
    right_index=True,
)
print(df.shape)   # (4992, 42)

# Add a Cosmos-level region id, which the probe figure colours by.
# BrainRegions ships inside iblatlas — no download.
br = BrainRegions()
df["Cosmos_id"] = br.remap(
    df["atlas_id"].to_numpy(), source_map="Allen", target_map="Cosmos"
)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use `BrainRegions`, not `ClassifierAtlas`, for plotting

`ephysatlas.data.read_features_from_disk` does this merge and mapping for you, but it
needs a `brain_atlas` and defaults to `ClassifierAtlas()`, which downloads the Allen
template volumes — hundreds of megabytes you do not need to draw a figure.
`BrainRegions` alone is enough to map and colour region ids, and it ships with
`iblatlas`. The IBL documentation covers it in
[working with the atlas](https://docs.internationalbrainlab.org/notebooks_external/atlas_working_with_ibllib_atlas.html)
and the Allen, Beryl and Cosmos mappings in
[atlas mapping](https://docs.internationalbrainlab.org/notebooks_external/atlas_mapping.html).
:::

## Features down one probe

`figure_features_channel_space` draws one panel per feature, each channel a rectangle at
its true position on the probe, coloured by feature value — with the brain regions beside
it for reference:

```python
import ephysatlas.plots

pid = df.index.get_level_values("pid").unique()[0]
pid_df = df[df.index.get_level_values("pid") == pid].copy()

# Channel positions: lateral (x) then axial (y), in micrometres
xy = pid_df[["lateral_um", "axial_um"]].to_numpy()

features = ["rms_lf", "psd_delta", "psd_theta", "psd_gamma", "rms_ap", "spike_count"]

fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.figure_features_channel_space(
    pid_df, features=features, xy=xy, pid=pid, br=br, mapping="Cosmos"
)
fig.savefig("features_along_probe.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

![Six features down a single probe, beside the Cosmos-level brain regions. Depth increases downwards; the probe tip is at the bottom. Most features change at the region boundaries, which is what region decoding relies on.](../figures/features_along_probe.png){.lightbox}

Read it left to right: the region labels and their Allen colours, the same regions as
unique-colour bands, then one strip per feature. This probe passes through Isocortex,
CNU, CTXsp and OLF, and `rms_lf`, `psd_delta` and `rms_ap` all shift visibly at those
transitions.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `xy` must be ordered lateral-then-axial

`xy` is an `[n_channels, 2]` array whose **first** column is `lateral_um` and **second**
is `axial_um`. Swap them and the figure renders without an error but places every channel
at the wrong position.
:::

### Choosing what to show

- **`features`** — any list of column names in `pid_df`. Panels appear in the order you
  give. Four to eight is comfortable; beyond that the panels get thin.
- **`mapping`** — the region map to colour by, `"Cosmos"` (coarse, 13 classes) or
  `"Beryl"` (finer). The function looks for a `{mapping}_id` column, so remap first as
  shown above.
- **`br=None`** — omit the brain regions entirely. The three region panels are blanked and
  you get features only.
- **`cmap`** — any matplotlib colormap name. Defaults to `"viridis"`.

### Comparable colour scales

By default each panel scales its colours to its own min/max, so panels are **not**
comparable to each other. Pin `vmin` / `vmax` to compare the same feature across probes:

```python
fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.figure_features_channel_space(
    pid_df, features=["rms_lf"], xy=xy, pid=pid, br=br, mapping="Cosmos",
    vmin=-95.0, vmax=-70.0,
)
```

Or pass a fitted `scaler` (anything with a `.transform` method, e.g. an sklearn
`StandardScaler`) to z-score the features before display, which puts features with very
different units on one visual footing:

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler().fit(df[features])
fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.figure_features_channel_space(
    pid_df, features=features, xy=xy, pid=pid, br=br, mapping="Cosmos",
    scaler=scaler,
)
```

Fit the scaler on the **whole** dataset, not one probe, or you have just removed the
between-probe differences you wanted to see.

### Looping over probes

```python
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

outdir = Path("figures")
outdir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

for pid in df.index.get_level_values("pid").unique():
    pid_df = df[df.index.get_level_values("pid") == pid].copy()
    fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.figure_features_channel_space(
        pid_df,
        features=features,
        xy=pid_df[["lateral_um", "axial_um"]].to_numpy(),
        pid=pid,
        br=br,
        mapping="Cosmos",
    )
    fig.savefig(outdir / f"{pid}.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.close(fig)   # or you will hold every figure in memory
```

## All features as one heatmap

Strips get thin beyond eight features. To see every feature of a probe at once,
`figure_features_heatmap` z-scores each feature over the whole dataset and draws the probe
as an image, one row per channel sorted by depth and one column per feature, beside the
histology:

```python
feature_groups = {
    "LF": ["rms_lf", "psd_delta", "psd_theta", "psd_alpha", "psd_beta", "psd_gamma", "psd_lfp"],
    "CSD": ["rms_lf_csd", "psd_delta_csd", "psd_theta_csd", "psd_alpha_csd",
            "psd_beta_csd", "psd_gamma_csd", "psd_lfp_csd"],
    "AP": ["rms_ap", "cor_ratio"],
    "Spikes": ["spike_count", "alpha_mean", "alpha_std", "peak_val", "trough_val", "tip_val",
               "depolarisation_slope", "repolarisation_slope", "recovery_slope", "polarity"],
}

pid = "dab512bd-a02d-4c1f-8dbc-9155a163efc0"   # crosses Isocortex, HPF and TH

fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.figure_features_heatmap(
    df_features, pid, channels=df_channels, feature_groups=feature_groups
)
```

![Probe `dab512bd` as a z-scored heatmap: 26 features (columns), grouped by band, against depth, beside the histology. The LF and CSD bands light up in the hippocampus (HPF) and drop in the thalamus (TH), and the spike features change at the same boundaries.](../figures/features_zscored_along_probe.png){.lightbox}

The histology bar takes the channel table's Allen `atlas_id` and draws it at the Cosmos
level (`mapping`). Leave out `feature_groups` to draw every feature the table has, grouped
by family: LF, CSD, AP and spikes.

Two defaults matter. The mean and standard deviation of the z-score are taken over every
probe of the table, for the same reason as the scaler above; pass `mean` and `std` to use
other statistics. And the colour range is clipped at ±2 (`vmin`, `vmax`): the LF and CSD
power of the hippocampus is several standard deviations above the rest of the brain and
would otherwise wash out every other contrast.

Each part of the figure can be turned off with `show_histology`, `show_colorbar`,
`show_group_labels` and `show_feature_names`. The axes come back by name
(`axs["histology"]`, `axs["features"]`, `axs["colorbar"]`), to adjust them afterwards.

### Before and after denoising

The same heatmap over the aggregated table (`raw_ephys_features.pqt`) and over the
denoised one shows what the total-variation filter does: channel-to-channel noise goes,
region boundaries stay sharp.

```python
from ephysatlas.features import EphysTransformer

features = [f for group in feature_groups.values() for f in group]
df_raw = pd.read_parquet(path / "raw_ephys_features.pqt")

# Same units as the denoised table, so the two panels share one colour scale
transformer = EphysTransformer()
transformer.fit(df_raw[features])
df_raw_t = transformer.transform(df_raw[features])

# One panel per table, both z-scored with the statistics of the first
fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.figure_features_heatmap(
    {"aggregated, before denoising": df_raw_t, "after denoising": df_features},
    pid,
    channels=df_channels,
    feature_groups=feature_groups,
    show_group_labels=False,
)
```

![Probe `dab512bd`, aggregated (left) and denoised (right), on one colour scale. The raw table was first put in the denoised units with `ephysatlas.features.EphysTransformer` (rms to dB, spike rate to log2), so the only difference left is the filter.](../figures/features_raw_vs_denoised.png){.lightbox}

See [aggregate and denoise](../how-to/aggregate-and-denoise.qmd) for the step itself.

## Feature distributions across a dataset

`plot_features_distributions` gives the complementary view — the marginal distribution of
each feature over every channel, with no depth information:

```python
features_24 = [
    "rms_lf", "psd_delta", "psd_theta", "psd_alpha", "psd_beta", "psd_gamma",
    "psd_lfp", "rms_lf_csd", "psd_delta_csd", "psd_theta_csd", "psd_alpha_csd",
    "psd_beta_csd", "psd_gamma_csd", "psd_lfp_csd", "rms_ap", "cor_ratio",
    "spike_count", "alpha_mean", "alpha_std", "peak_val", "trough_val",
    "tip_val", "depolarisation_slope", "repolarisation_slope",
]

fig, axs = ephysatlas.plots.plot_features_distributions(
    df, x_list=features_24,
    title="Feature distributions (2025_W28 fixture, 13 probes)",
)
fig.savefig("features_distributions.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

`peak_val` and `trough_val` exist in this `2025_W28` fixture, but not in the `2026_W42`
denoised tables, which carry the
[spike-shape columns](../reference/feature-list.qmd#spike-shape-columns) instead. On those
tables, plot `spike_amplitude` and `spike_width_secs` in their place.

![Marginal distribution of 24 features across 4992 channels from 13 probes. Bars are coloured by bin centre, and the axis limits use quantiles (0.5%–99.5%) so a few extreme channels cannot flatten the histogram.](../figures/features_distributions.png){.lightbox}

When a model gives unexpected results on your data, compare your distributions with
these: a units problem or a badly scaled feature shows up as a shifted distribution.

::: {.callout-note}
## Pass 24 features to fill the grid

The layout is a fixed 4×6 grid of histogram-plus-colorbar pairs, so it holds exactly 24
features. Fewer leaves blank panels; **more than 24 raises `IndexError`** — split the
list across several calls instead. Features absent from the DataFrame are skipped with a
warning rather than raising, and do not consume a panel.

Omit `x_list` entirely and it uses `ephysatlas.features.voltage_features_set()`.
:::

### The values are in denoised units

Note the scales above: `rms_lf` sits near −90 and `psd_*` between −100 and −210, because
`raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt` stores `rms_ap` and `rms_lf` in **dB** and
`spike_count` in **log2**. Plot
`raw_ephys_features.pqt` instead and `rms_lf` comes out in volts, around 1e-5.

The two are not comparable, so a model trained on denoised features must be given
denoised features. See
[aggregate and denoise](../how-to/aggregate-and-denoise.qmd).

## Troubleshooting

**`KeyError: 'Cosmos_id'`** — `figure_features_channel_space` looks for a
`{mapping}_id` column. Add it with `br.remap(...)` as shown, or pass `br=None` to skip
the region panels.

**The figure is drawn but channels are in the wrong places** — `xy` columns are swapped.
Lateral first, axial second.

**A feature panel is uniformly one colour** — that feature is constant or all-NaN for this
probe. Check `pid_df[feature].describe()`.

**Warnings that a feature was not found and skipped** — `plot_features_distributions`
skips missing columns rather than raising. Check the names against `df.columns`.

**Nothing renders in a script** — matplotlib needs a backend. In a headless environment
set `matplotlib.use("Agg")` before importing `pyplot` and save to file rather than calling
`plt.show()`.
